item.title: Palau president meets with UAE leaders ahead of UN climate change talks

item.content:encoded:
Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr. has been discussing climate change with officials in the United Arab Emirates ahead of the 31 st United Nations Climate Change Conference, which begins in Turkey this week.

Whipps, who is serving as the chairperson of the Pacific Islands Forum, was accompanied by Forum Secretary General Baron Divavesi Waqa for a meeting with the UAE’s President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Discussions focused on strengthening cooperation, advancing key Pacific regional priorities ahead of the UN conference, and exploring opportunities to deepen collaboration on climate finance.

Whipps also met with the United Arab Emirates’ Minister of Climate Change and Environment Amna bint Abdullah Al Dahak Al Shamsi to discuss how the UAE’s investment capacity and expertise in renewable energy, climate-resilient infrastructure and water security could support practical partnerships with Palau and the wider Pacific.

The meeting highlighted a key Pacific priority: securing contributions to the Pacific Resilience Facility—the first Pacific-led and Pacific-owned regional financing facility dedicated to strengthening the resilience of Pacific communities.

Whipps was in the United Arab Emirates leading the high-level Pacific Islands Forum mission to strengthen cooperation on climate resilience, investment and sustainable development.

item.title: New CNMI PSS lawsuit revives constitutional battle over school funding

item.content:encoded:
The CNMI Public School System has returned to court in a renewed fight over constitutionally mandated education funding, suing Gov. David M. Apatang and acting Finance Secretary Natalia M. Sablan over what it alleges is an unlawful budget formula that deprives public schools of nearly $12 million in fiscal year 2027 funding.

The complaint, filed Oct. 30 in Superior Court by PSS through Interim Commissioner of Education Jacqueline P. Che, seeks declaratory and injunctive relief and asks the court to order a recalculation of the Commonwealth's constitutional funding obligation to public education.

Summonses have been issued to Apatang and Sablan in their official capacities, requiring them to respond to the lawsuit through the Office of the Attorney General.

At the center of the dispute is an article of the CNMI Constitution that guarantees public elementary and secondary education an annual appropriation of no less than 25% of the Commonwealth's general revenues.

PSS argues that the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Plan Act improperly reduces the revenue base used to calculate that constitutional funding requirement by deducting debt-service payments and other obligations before determining the amount owed to public schools.

The lawsuit revives a legal battle that previously reached the CNMI Supreme Court during litigation between PSS and the administration of former Gov. Ralph DLG Torres. In a landmark 2020 decision, the high court ruled that revenues may be excluded from the constitutional funding calculation only when they qualify as special revenues and have a sufficient connection between the source of the funds and the purpose for which they are restricted.

PSS contends the current budget methodology conflicts with that ruling by treating debt-service obligations as deductions from general revenues before calculating the school system's constitutional share.

According to court filings, the FY 2027 budget identifies about $152.8 million in budgetary resources. After deducting special-revenue earmarks and approximately $47.7 million in debt-service obligations, lawmakers calculated roughly $100.7 million as available for appropriation, resulting in an allocation of about $25 million to PSS.

The school system argues debt-service payments are expenditures rather than revenue classifications and therefore should not reduce the constitutional funding base. Under PSS's calculations, the base should total roughly $148.4 million, entitling the school system to approximately $37.1 million. The lawsuit alleges the current budget leaves a shortfall of at least $11.9 million.

Court documents note that Apatang's original budget proposal included approximately $37.1 million for PSS. However, lawmakers ultimately appropriated about $25 million.

PSS said it is not seeking to interfere with debt-service payments, pension obligations or other legally required expenditures. Instead, it is asking the court to determine the proper constitutional funding level and ensure sufficient revenues are available to satisfy the mandate.

The complaint warns the alleged shortfall could force reductions in instructional time, employee work hours, staffing and student services during the current fiscal year.

PSS is seeking declarations that portions of the FY 2027 budget law are unconstitutional, an expedited hearing and an injunction preventing the expenditure of certain general revenues until the dispute is resolved.

As of Thursday, no responses had been filed by the governor or the Department of Finance.

item.title: Ada-Calvo administration to open government positions to public applicants
item.description: Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation. During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an o
item.content:encoded:
Gov.-elect Tony Ada and Lt. Gov.-elect E.J. Calvo said their incoming administration will open cabinet and senior staff positions to public applicants, with an emphasis on professional experience, qualifications, and commitment to public service rather than political affiliation.

During their first press conference as governor and lieutenant governor-elect, the two outlined plans to establish an online application portal where interested residents, including current government employees, can submit resumes and apply for positions within the incoming administration.

Jadeen Perez, who will chair the transition team’s Committee on Administration and Appointees, said the committee plans to begin accepting applications after the election results are certified on Nov. 19.

Applicants will undergo background checks and an evaluation of their qualifications before the committee submits recommendations to Ada and Calvo.

Ada said the application process will be open to anyone interested in serving, including members of the current administration.

“The bottom line is, everybody working together, regardless of party affiliation,” Ada said. “Election is over. Now it’s time for everybody to come together and work together.”

The incoming administration has also established three principal transition committees to guide the transfer of government responsibilities. The Committee on Government Operations and Efficiency, chaired by Nate Denight, will review the operations of government agencies, identify opportunities to improve efficiency, and assess existing challenges. The Committee on Administration and Appointees will oversee the recruitment and evaluation of potential cabinet members and senior staff, while the Committee on Inaugural Arrangements, chaired by Piti Mayor Jesse Alig, will coordinate inauguration preparations.

Denight said the government operations committee will establish additional subcommittees to review the island’s 52 government agencies. The committees will meet with agency management and staff to identify what is working, what needs improvement, and what resources may be needed.

Their findings will be compiled into a final transition report outlining each department’s current situation, objectives, and recommendations. Transition chair Jerry Crisostomo said the report will help Ada and Calvo determine their administration’s priorities and guide appointments ahead of their expected Jan. 4 start in office.

Ada said the incoming administration will first focus on completing a smooth transition and assessing the government’s financial position and operational needs before determining its immediate priorities.

One policy direction the incoming administration has already identified is a dedicated executive leadership position for tourism and destination development, separate from economic development. Calvo said they may be the first administration ever to dedicate an executive position to the industry of tourism.

“The position we’re looking at is actually tourism and destination development, separate from economic development, which is important,” Calvo said, “I think that would probably have fallen under economic development in the past, but we need to look at diversifying our economy and also protecting other growing industries separately.”

Ada said the position would reflect tourism’s significant impact on Guam’s economy and employment, particularly as the island’s tourism industry continues to face challenges.

When asked about their first 100 days in office, Ada said the administration will begin implementing its campaign plans after evaluating the government’s needs and establishing its leadership team. Calvo identified tourism, economic development, federal relations, and education as among the areas that will require attention.

When asked what the new administration is most excited to begin working on as they work toward a smooth government transition, they said they plan to continue monthly community cleanups, which began during the campaign.

“We want to still get out there and keep our community clean,” Ada said. “We want to ensure that, as we continue to move along within the first 100 days of our administration, that we start implementing our plans and get it to what we said during our campaign. You’re going to start seeing the implementation of those plans come to fruition.”

Ada and Calvo said they will seek guidance from former Republican governors and lieutenant governors to assist with the transition. Those invited to serve as honorary transition advisers include former governors Felix Camacho and Eddie Calvo, along with former lieutenant governors Ray Tenorio, Mike Cruz and Kaleo Moylan.

The transition team says additional appointments and opportunities for public participation will be announced in the coming weeks. Updates are expected through the incoming administration’s website and social media platforms.

item.title: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats

item.content:encoded:
Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.

It's a stunning shift from 2024 , when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.

But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.

Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.

However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.

The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.

When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.

But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.

Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.

Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.

Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees .

Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.

"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."

Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll , notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.

"I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."

By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate , a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.

"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.

"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

item.title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
item.description: Updated November 8, 2026 at 6:45 PM ChST Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 8, 2026 at 6:45 PM ChST

Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.

President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday. Herzog made the decision after parties representing most of the members of Israel's parliament recommended Eisenkot to try forming a governing coalition.

Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages.

Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.

He leads the center-right Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.

That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

The coalition building promises to be a tough task and could include strange bedfellows: from ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to Arab-led parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel — who make up about 20% of Israel and had a record turnout in these elections.

They could now potentially be the kingmakers. But both Eisenkot and Netanyahu ruled out working with them before the elections. Now there's some public pressure on Eisenkot to change his mind, and on Saturday Netanyahu issued a video warning against that.

He said it would be partnering with what he called Hamas supporters and "those who oppose Judaism." Eisenkot responded, calling Netanyahu's video hysterical.

If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

item.title: Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say
item.description: Updated November 8, 2026 at 11:01 AM ChST KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 8, 2026 at 11:01 AM ChST

KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.

The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow's Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.

The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn't release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.

Four women and two men were killed in the Krakow attack. At least three of the women were Polish, and one of the dead was a U.K. citizen, authorities said. Police were still trying to identify the other two people who were killed.

A total of 13 people were hospitalized in serious condition, authorities said, though that figure may include the gunman, who underwent surgery after the attack.

It's unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the mass shooting. Two police officers were seriously injured, Kierwiński said. Five non-Poles were also injured, police commander Marek Boroń said.

People were wounded at several locations

The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.

The attacker engaged in a "wild ride" around Main Square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, said Cisło, adding that the gunman appears to have acted alone.

Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.

"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted on X.

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground.

Photos showed a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter after it landed in the square.

It wasn't immediately clear whether the gun used in the attack or those found in the attacker's car are legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days , leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children.

The Krakow attacker's military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague. "We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski announced increased security measures, including road barriers, along main streets in the old town in the Polish capital in the aftermath of the Krakow attack.

item.title: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
item.description: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money. Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers
item.content:encoded:
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money.

Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population.

He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.

Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.

A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning . The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012.

Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation . Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process.

At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website .

Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest .

"I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you," Peña said in a speech posted to social media.

Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, was sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028. In a speech on Friday , he announced he would take action to compensate people whose money was lost in the bank's collapse.

Paraguay's central bank said it seized control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday because its solvency ratio, an assessment of a company's long-term financial viability, no longer met legal standards.

Protests erupted across Asunción , the country's capital city, following the seizure.

NPR's John Otis and Catherine Osborn contributed reporting to this story.
